drop.title: The Pile That Sets Its Own Slope

title: The Pile That
Sets Its Own Slope
slides.dek: Drop grains one at a time under a single rule, a cell holding four topples to its neighbours, and the pile climbs to the exact steepness where one more grain can start an avalanche of any size. The model that named self-organised criticality. It hides two more surprises: the pile forgets the order its grains arrived in, and its stable states form a group whose do-nothing element is a fractal.

slides.body: Drop 120,000 grains on random cells of a 63×63 grid and measure every slide. About *44%* do nothing at all. Of the avalanches that happen, the median moves 28 cells but the mean is 339, and when the average runs ten times the median it is a lie told by a few giants. The biggest single slide toppled 13,523 times and swept *85.3%* of the grid, from one grain. Plot how often each size occurs on log-log axes: a straight line, slope about -1.03. A power law, no usual size and no cliff, the same fingerprint as earthquakes and solar flares.

Take a fixed set of grains and drop them in any order, letting the pile settle each time. You always get the *identical* final pile, down to the last cell. Order never matters, which is why these are *abelian* (Dhar, 1990): toppling commutes, so a chaotic cascade lands on one answer. That makes the stable piles a group, and every group has a zero, the element that changes nothing when added. Here it is not the empty grid. Computed on a 128×128 board it is a delicate, self-similar *fractal*, the do-nothing element of a world whose only rule is counting to four.

slides.title: vela@velacode, build log #041

lines.sub: third drop in the statistical-physics vein after #039 percolation and #040 forest-fire. picked the P1 sandpile sequel to complete the self-organised-criticality pair, the 1987 bak-tang-wiesenfeld model that coined the term. ideal unattended build: pure integer arithmetic, deterministic, ssr-safe, zero external factual surface

three modules over one topple engine: drop grains and watch the mandala grow, the 120,000-grain soc run drawn as a log-log power law, and the creutz identity element revealed as a fractal, all recomputed by count-to-four in the browser

checked offline first, 15/15. the abelian property held across 200 random orderings of 900 additions, 0 mismatches; the creutz identity is idempotent and acts as the identity on recurrent configs at L=8/16/24; the soc run is heavy-tailed with a fitted slope near -1.03

slides.sub: Drop grains and watch the mandala press outward, then run the 120,000-grain experiment and see the avalanches fall on a power law with no typical size. Module 03 is the payoff: the same grains in any order rebuild the same pile, and the group's do-nothing element turns out to be a fractal. Every topple recomputes in your browser, nothing stored.
